title: Which test cases should you automate vs leave manual (automate the repetitive, stable, business-critical, time-consuming, frequently-run, data-driven, regression-suitable ones; keep exploratory, one-off, highly-volatile, or UX-judgement checks manual), and why is "automate everything because we can" a mistake (unstable requirements → brittle, high-maintenance tests)?
shortTitle: Which test cases to automate vs leave manual, and why "automate everything" is a mistake
keyPoints: Automate tests that are repetitive, stable, business-critical, frequently run, data-driven, and regression-suitable
Keep manual: exploratory testing, one-off checks, features with volatile requirements, and tests requiring human judgement
Automation has an up-front build cost and ongoing maintenance cost that must be recovered through repeated runs
Automating volatile features produces brittle tests that break on every legitimate change, eroding trust in the suite
Automating judgement-based checks like visual aesthetics gives false confidence when tests pass while UX is broken
Treat the automation suite as a product: prioritize by risk, measure flakiness, and retire tests that no longer earn their keep

s1_definition.oneliner: Automate the repetitive, stable, business-critical, frequently run, data-driven, regression tests, and keep exploratory, one-off, volatile, and judgement-based checks manual, because automating unstable or low-value tests just builds a brittle, expensive suite nobody trusts.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Good automation candidates** – Repetitive tests that run on every build, stable features with rarely changing behavior, business-critical paths where a regression is catastrophic, time-consuming manual checks, data-driven tests with many input rows, and regression tests that protect existing behavior.
- **Poor automation candidates** – Exploratory testing where value is human adaptability, one-off checks that run once, features with volatile requirements that change every sprint, and tests requiring human judgement like visual aesthetics or usability.
- **"Automate everything" trap** – Automating unstable features creates brittle tests that break on legitimate changes, inflating maintenance cost until the team fixes tests instead of finding bugs, and eroding trust when failures are ignored.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, some checks happen the same way every single day, like confirming a transfer of fifty thousand rupees debits and credits correctly; writing a robot to do those pays off hugely because it runs on every build forever. But some checks are one-time, like verifying a brand-new experimental screen whose design changes weekly, or need a human's eye, like whether the new statement layout looks trustworthy and reads clearly. Trying to build robots for those is wasteful: the robot breaks every week when the screen changes, and no robot can judge whether a layout feels trustworthy. A wise team automates the stable, repetitive, money-critical checks and keeps a skilled human for exploration and judgement.

```text
  Automation Decision Matrix
  ──────────────────────────

                    Stable            Volatile
                 ┌──────────────┬──────────────┐
  Business-      │  AUTOMATE    │  DEFER until │
  Critical       │  NOW         │  it settles  │
                 ├──────────────┼──────────────┤
  Low-Value /    │  Automate if │  KEEP MANUAL │
  One-Off        │  repetitive  │              │
                 └──────────────┴──────────────┘

  Requires human judgement?  ──> Always KEEP MANUAL
```

```text
  "Automate Everything" vs Balanced Strategy
  ───────────────────────────────────────────

  "Automate everything":           Balanced:
  ┌────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────┐
  │ 500 automated tests│          │ 200 automated tests│
  │ 150 flaky          │          │ 5 flaky            │
  │ 30% ignored        │          │ 0% ignored         │
  │ 40 hrs/wk maint    │          │ 4 hrs/wk maint     │
  │ Trust: LOW         │          │ Trust: HIGH        │
  └────────────────────┘          └────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Deciding what to automate is a cost-benefit judgement, because automation has an up-front cost to write and an ongoing cost to maintain, and it returns value every time it runs without human effort. I automate where the lifetime savings beat the lifetime cost: repetitive tests that run on every build, stable features whose behavior rarely changes, business-critical paths like transfer and payment where a regression is catastrophic, time-consuming manual checks that become cheap data-driven loops, and regression tests that protect existing behavior.

I keep manual the exploratory testing where a skilled human follows hunches, one-off checks that run once, features whose requirements are still volatile, and anything requiring human judgement like whether a layout looks trustworthy. The reason "automate everything" is a mistake is that automation value is not uniform: automating volatile features produces brittle tests that break on every legitimate change, and when tests fail for the wrong reasons people start ignoring failures, which destroys the suite's credibility exactly when a real regression appears.

At the National Bank of India I treated the automation suite as a product. I automated the transfer and payment regression and the interest calculation as a data-driven test over hundreds of rows, saving days of manual effort every release. But I deliberately did not automate a new rewards screen that changed weekly, and I kept statement-layout review manual because no assertion can judge whether a layout feels trustworthy. I tracked flakiness and retired tests that no longer earned their keep.

Remember one sentence: automate the stable, critical, repetitive core aggressively, defer the volatile, and keep the judgemental manual, because a trusted suite of 200 stable tests beats a brittle suite of 500 that nobody believes.
